## Problem 1

```{r load_noaa}
data("ny_noaa")

ny_noaa
```

```{r noaa_missingness}
ny_noaa |>
  summarize(across(everything(), ~ mean(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "proportion_missing"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r noaa_overview}
ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    n_stations = n_distinct(id),
    first_date = min(date),
    last_date = max(date)
  )
```

The ny_noaa dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables, representing daily weather records from 747 stations in New York State between 1981 and 2010. Each row represents a station on a particular date. Variables include station ID (id), date (date), precipitation (prcp), snowfall (snow), snow depth (snwd), and maximum and minimum temperatures (tmax and tmin). Missing data are substantial, particularly for temperature: approximately 43.7% of both maximum and minimum temperature values are missing. Precipitation, snowfall, and snow depth are approximately 5.6%, 14.7%, and 22.8% missing, respectively. These gaps limit the observations available for each analysis.

```{r clean_noaa}
noaa_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )

noaa_df
```

```{r snowfall_counts}
noaa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

I created separate year, month, and day variables, converted temperatures to numeric values in degrees Celsius, and converted precipitation to millimeters. Snowfall and snow depth were retained in millimeters. The most common snowfall value is 0 mm, appearing in 2,008,508 observations, which is expected because most days have no snowfall. The next most common values are 25, 13, and 51 mm. These are approximately 1, 0.5, and 2 inches, suggesting that measurements recorded in inches were converted to millimeters and rounded.

```{r january_july_temperature, fig.width=8, fig.asp=.6}
noaa_monthly_df =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7), !is.na(tmax)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )

noaa_monthly_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3, size = .8) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average daily maximum temperature by station",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean maximum temperature (°C)"
  )
```

```{r july_outlier}
noaa_monthly_df |>
  filter(month == "July") |>
  arrange(mean_tmax) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)
```

```{r check_july_outlier}
noaa_df |>
  filter(id == "USC00308962", year == 1988, month == 7) |>
  summarize(
    recorded_days = n(),
    days_with_tmax = sum(!is.na(tmax)),
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_tmax = min(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_tmax = max(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

July has much higher average maximum temperatures than January, reflecting seasonal differences. Stations also vary within each year, and January shows more pronounced year-to-year fluctuations than July. An unusually low July average occurs at station USC00308962 in 1988, at approximately 13.95°C. All 31 days have maximum temperature records, so missing days do not explain this outlier. Further investigation would be needed to determine whether it reflects actual conditions or a recording issue.

```{r temperature_snowfall_plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=10}
temperature_plot =
  noaa_df |>
  drop_na(tmin, tmax) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 60) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
  breaks = c(5000, 10000, 15000),
  labels = c("5k", "10k", "15k")
) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily minimum and maximum temperatures",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  )

snowfall_plot =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of snowfall by year",
    subtitle = "Days with snowfall greater than 0 and less than 100 mm",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = .5))

temperature_plot / snowfall_plot
```

Minimum and maximum daily temperatures show a strong positive association: days with higher minimum temperatures generally have higher maximum temperatures. Some extreme values and observations where the maximum is below the minimum suggest possible recording issues. Among days with snowfall greater than 0 and less than 100 mm, distributions are fairly similar across years, with medians near 25 mm and some variation in spread. There is no obvious consistent trend over time within this restricted range.

## Problem 2

```{r clean_nhanes_demographics}
nhanes_covar_df =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  drop_na() |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )

nhanes_covar_df
```

```{r tidy_merge_nhanes}
nhanes_accel_df =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(minute = as.integer(minute))

nhanes_df =
  inner_join(nhanes_covar_df, nhanes_accel_df, by = "seqn")

nhanes_df |>
  summarize(
    n_participants = n_distinct(seqn),
    n_observations = n()
  )
```

```{r education_sex_table}
nhanes_df |>
  distinct(seqn, sex, education) |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Education level", "Male", "Female"),
    caption = "Number of participants by education level and sex"
  )
```

```{r age_distributions, fig.width=8, fig.asp=.6}
nhanes_df |>
  distinct(seqn, sex, age, education) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 1, labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 20)) +
  labs(
    title = "Age distributions by sex and education",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

After excluding participants younger than 21 and those with missing demographic data, 228 participants remained. I encoded sex and education as factors, reshaped the activity measurements into one row per participant per minute, and merged the datasets using participant ID. The largest education category is more than high school, with 56 men and 59 women. Counts are similar by sex in the other categories except high school equivalent, which includes 35 men and 23 women. Age distributions overlap substantially between sexes. Participants with more than high school education generally have lower median ages, while women in the high school equivalent group have a higher median age than men.

```{r total_activity_age, fig.width=8, fig.asp=.6}
nhanes_total_df =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(mims),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

nhanes_total_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ education,
    nrow = 1,
    labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 20)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity by age, sex, and education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total daily activity (summed MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Total daily activity generally decreases with age, although the relationship is nonlinear and varies by education level and sex. Women tend to have higher activity than men across much of the age range in the high school equivalent and more than high school groups. In the less than high school group, the curves cross, with men showing higher activity around ages 50–65. There is substantial individual variation, including a participant with unusually low total activity in the more than high school group. These patterns are descriptive and do not establish causal effects of age, sex, or education.

```{r activity_time_course, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
nhanes_time_df =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarize(mean_mims = mean(mims), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(hour = (minute - 1) / 60)

nhanes_time_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, span = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~education,
    nrow = 1,
    labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 20)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 6, 12, 18, 24),
    labels = c("00:00", "06:00", "12:00", "18:00", "24:00")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Activity throughout the day by education and sex",
    x = "Time of day",
    y = "Mean activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

The graph shows that activity is lowest overnight, rises sharply in the morning, and declines in the evening across all three education groups. In addition, men and women have similar daytime activity in the less than high school group. Finally, we can also observe that women generally have higher daytime activity in the other two groups, with the clearest difference in the more than high school group.

## Problem 3

```{r citibike_import}
jan_2020_df =
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "January")

july_2020_df =
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "July")

jan_2024_df =
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "January")

july_2024_df =
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")

citibike_df =
  bind_rows(
    jan_2020_df,
    july_2020_df,
    jan_2024_df,
    july_2024_df
  ) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
        "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual", "member"),
      labels = c("Casual", "Member")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type)
  )

glimpse(citibike_df)
```

The dataset contains 99,485 rides and 9 variables, with one ride per row. The data cover January and July of 2020 and 2024, with a 1% sample of rides lasting less than four hours in each month. The dataset records ride ID, bike type, weekday, duration, starting and ending stations, membership status, year, and month. I standardized column names, added year and month, combined the four files, and converted categorical variables to factors.

```{r citibike_ride_counts}
citibike_df |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  arrange(year, month) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Year", "Month", "Casual rides", "Member rides"),
    caption = "Number of sampled Citi Bike rides by year, month, and membership"
  )
```

The table shows that member rides outnumber casual rides in all four months. Both groups have more rides in July than January in each year, and both have more rides in 2024 than in the same month of 2020. Lastly, July 2024 has the most sampled rides, with 47,156.
